## TL;DR

Closed the review evidence gap for the Agents tabs QA pass. Captured Build Your Team, Scheduled Tasks, Reminders, and Detected Coding Agents at 1280×900 and 375×812 using headless Playwright against the auth-less server running from a detached scratch worktree. The page stayed within the viewport at both sizes. Added screenshot links and a specific scheduled-list failure capture to the QA note. While reproducing the requested failure evidence, found and fixed a real schedule loading error gap: failed requests now appear as an announced alert instead of an empty state. The direct preview server is read-only, so save/reload persistence is still evidenced only through the prior in-memory API stub, not through actual filesystem writes.

## Work and rationale

The latest review report classified the first pass as evidence-gap-only. It said the automatic capture showed Mission Control at `/`, while the task concerns four tabs on `/agents`; it found no code bugs. The reviewer asked for desktop and mobile captures, relevant empty or error states, and evidence that edits persist across reloads. I treated the reported issue as a request for concrete evidence rather than changing the visual design of the tabs.

The second review found that the declared shots were still absent from handoff evidence and that the report draft did not reflect the checked tree. I refreshed the three tab shot declarations through `repoos update`, retained the tab-specific desktop/mobile screenshots in the QA note, and refreshed this report against the current checked tree. The second handoff check also reported that its reused check inputs had changed during finalization; I ran a fresh unscoped `repoos check` after the review return. That run completed with all checks passing, including remote build and the full test suite.

I reran the browser work in a detached scratch worktree, with `just serve-noauth 7278`, then used Playwright in headless mode. No visible browser or user Chrome profile was opened. The capture script visited the four tab deep links and the existing fixtures (`agents:empty`, `agents:scheduledSeeded`, `reminders:due`, and `agents:lastRuns`) at 1280×900 and 375×812. It recorded `document.documentElement.scrollWidth` equal to the viewport width for each route and size. Images sit next to the QA note under `docs/qa/2026-11-agents-tabs/`; the note links each desktop/mobile pair. I also declared three review shots for the team, scheduled, and reminders panels, using their real routes and the existing tab container as the highlight.

The review asks for edits surviving reload. The previous browser run exercised team instruction, schedule create/edit, and reminder create/edit flows with an in-memory API stub that persisted mocked responses between reloads. The checks passed at the stated viewport sizes. The preview server rejects non-GET requests with HTTP 405, so real server persistence cannot be demonstrated through this auth-less preview. The QA note states that limitation explicitly. I did not change the server or write to schedule/reminder data to bypass its read-only policy.

To make the scheduled error surface concrete, I intercepted the schedule GET with a 503 and captured the result. That exposed a behavior not identified in the review: `refreshSchedules()` caught and discarded errors, after which the panel could display “No schedules yet.” That is misleading because the list failed to load. I changed the store to retain the latest fetch error and clear it after a successful fetch. The panel now announces the load failure with `role="alert"` and suppresses the empty-list copy until loading succeeds. A regression test drives a 503 JSON error through the store and verifies the alert replaces the empty state. The existing save and update error paths remain separate and continue to use their inline alert surface.

## Approaches tried

The initial screenshot script captured all four pages and measured widths, but its first schedule error attempt ran against the scratch build from before the error-state fix. The expected alert did not appear, confirming the running bundle was stale relative to the task worktree. I copied only the changed store and panel source into the scratch worktree, forced its UI build, and reran the capture. All eight tab/viewport captures completed, and the 503 test then observed “Could not load scheduled tasks: schedule service unavailable.”

I retained the in-memory API-stub persistence checks from the prior QA run rather than presenting successful browser responses as proof of real disk persistence. For this rerun, I focused the added visual evidence on the exact page and state the review could not see. The scheduled error screenshot supplements the two-size tab matrix without implying that a mocked service failure is a live backend result.

## Challenges and blockers

The preview server is intentionally read-only. It returned HTTP 405 for direct schedule and reminder writes, which blocks end-to-end verification of durable server-side saves. The mock persistence workflow can only prove that the UI handles successful responses and renders retained values after reload; it cannot prove the server wrote those values to disk. This limit is recorded in the QA note for the reviewer.

The scratch worktree initially served its already-built UI. Copying the latest panel/store files and forcing a rebuild was necessary before the schedule error screenshot reflected the current code. I stopped the server and removed the detached scratch worktree after capturing evidence.

## Key learnings

A screenshot is useful review evidence only when its route and state match the requested surface. A generic app landing-page capture can be clean and still say nothing about a specific tab. Tab deep links and named fixtures make the evidence direct and repeatable, while reporting measured viewport widths makes the mobile overflow claim checkable.

The scheduled list also showed why empty and error states must remain distinct. If a failed request is swallowed, a useful empty-state invitation becomes a false claim that no schedules exist. Keeping the load error in the store lets the panel explain the failure and avoids conflating unavailable data with an empty collection. Finally, tests and browser evidence should distinguish mocked persistence from actual storage; the latter remains constrained by the preview server’s read-only behavior.
